summary: Kickoff for a 3-week POC to validate quality and performance for an internal research-assistant feature. Agreed success metrics (latency, throughput, hallucination tolerance), a benchmark plan (golden prompts + regression suite), workload sizing, and an initial timeline with owners. Follow-ups: Redwood to deliver harness and SOW; Pinnacle to share sample queries and infra constraints.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right good morning everyone thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood. Quick intro: Ethan is our solutions engineer, Lina from CSM will help on onboarding ops.
[00:14] Rajiv Menon: Hey thanks, Rajiv here CTO at Pinnacle. We're trying to scope a short POC to validate model quality and operational cost before we commit to dedicated infra.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Great, can you give a bit more context on the feature?
[00:32] Sofia Alvarez: Sure, it's an internal research assistant — ingesting internal papers and query rewriting, summarization and cite-back. Typical prompt lengths are 50 to 400 tokens, with some multi-turn threads. Our current traffic is small, but expected burstiness during team runs.
[00:46] Ethan Park: When you say burstiness what does that look like? qps or concurrent users?
[00:50] Tom Harris: For Notebook runs, we get short spikes of 30 to 80 concurrent sessions, about 200 requests over a 2 minute window sometimes. Day average is maybe 5 to 10 qps.
[01:05] Ethan Park: Okay useful. For the POC we usually do a functional quality eval plus a load sweep. Suggested initial load targets: steady 10 qps with bursts to 80 qps for 2 minutes, and a pure token-throughput run to validate cost. Does that align?
[01:21] Sofia Alvarez: Yes that sounds fine. Also important — hallucination tolerance: we need <2% critical hallucinations on our benchmark set, and output structure must pass schema checks for citations.
[01:32] Maya Chen: Good to note. Let's write that down as a success metric: critical hallucinations <2% on golden set; structural validity 99% (JSON citations schema); p95 latency under 600ms for hosted lane and under 350ms for dedicated lane. Does that map to your expectations?
[01:48] Rajiv Menon: p95 350ms for dedicated is optimistic but acceptable as a target, yes. Cost targets: not exceed $0.015 per 1k tokens in POC measurement — that will determine whether we go dedicated.
[02:01] Ethan Park: Ok we'll measure cost both as per-token and per-request CPU/GPU utilization. For the quality plan, our approach is three parts: golden prompts (gold set), regression tests (auto scored), and hallucination / format checks.
[02:14] Maya Chen: Walk us through the golden prompts piece.
[02:16] Ethan Park: Golden set: we ask you to provide 150-250 representative queries across use cases — retrieval, summarization, cite-back, rewriting. We'll pair them with expected outputs or evaluation rubrics. We'll use both automated metrics (ROUGE / BERTScore where useful) and manual spot checks. These will be the canonical regression cases for the POC and later onboarding.
[02:36] Sofia Alvarez: We can put that together. Note, some queries reference proprietary paper IDs and we need to mask PII, but maintain context.
[02:43] Ethan Park: That's fine; anonymized samples are OK. For hallucination detection we'll run a citation-extraction step and compare against the retrieval index to detect unsupported claims. That will surface false-positives and we can label them.
[02:57] Tom Harris: On the infra side, network: we plan VPC peering for the private lane. For hosted runs during POC we need to restrict egress to our IP allowlist. Is that supported?
[03:07] Maya Chen: Yes we support IP allowlisting and VPC peering. SE pairing will validate firewall/NAT.
[03:12] Ethan Park: On scoring: each golden prompt will have a pass/fail for critical criteria (hallucination, citation presence, schema). Then a graded score for fluency and relevance 1-5. Acceptance rule: >=85% of golden prompts pass critical criteria and average relevance >=4.0.
[03:30] Sofia Alvarez: That acceptance threshold matches internal bar. How do you handle edge cases where output is correct but differently formatted?
[03:36] Ethan Park: We'll apply normalization rules (whitespace, citation order) and provide a schema/format validator; differences after normalization are considered non-critical.
[03:44] Rajiv Menon: What about regression cadence post-POC? We want nightly smoke runs on main branch and a weekly expanded run.
[03:51] Lina Rodriguez: We can set up a CI hook to run the regression suite nightly against a pinned model. For the POC we'll run daily regression and capture diffs in a report.
[04:01] Tom Harris: Load testing telemetry: what will you need us to provide?
[04:05] Ethan Park: We'll ask for sample traffic profile and a short-term token distribution. If you can provide 2 weeks of historical telemetry we'll synthesize realistic sequences including multi-turn context. If not, a 10k sample query set works.
[04:18] Sofia Alvarez: We can export that. We'll also include a small golden subset flagged for manual review.
[04:25] Maya Chen: Timeline proposal: Week 0 (this week) — align on scope; Week 1 — Redwood builds harness and pair with Pinnacle for infra; Week 2 — run functional golden tests + daily regressions; Week 3 — run load sweep, finalize report and SOW decision. Does 3 weeks work?
[04:41] Rajiv Menon: Tight but doable. We'd like a mid-point checkpoint after week 1 results.
[04:47] Ethan Park: We'll schedule a 30m check-in at the end of week 1 to review early metrics and any blocker.
[04:54] Sophia Alvarez: Quick question on model variants: will you test quantized variants and fallback routing?
[04:59] Ethan Park: Yes we'll include a baseline unquantized model and a quantized 4-bit variant to measure cost/perf tradeoffs. Routing fallbacks can be simulated by switching to a compatible model family and we will capture differences in the report.
[05:12] Tom Harris: Are there any limitations we should be aware of on streaming or function calls? We sometimes rely on function-style structured outputs.
[05:19] Maya Chen: Streaming and function-calling are supported; we recommend testing function calls as part of golden prompts. We'll include one function-output heavy subset.
[05:28] Rajiv Menon: Security ask — we need SOC2 and the audit log for any private deployment. Can you share the security pack?
[05:34] Lina Rodriguez: Yes I'll send the security deck and a redacted SOC2 summary. For private we provide audit log exports and KMS integrations; we will document flows in the SOW.
[05:44] Sofia Alvarez: On acceptance — if we hit latency but miss hallucination by a small margin how do you advise?
[05:51] Ethan Park: We prefer to prioritize quality for your use case. If latency is off but quality meets the bar, we can discuss batching and cache tuning to improve latency without sacrificing quality, and estimate cost impact.
[06:05] Tom Harris: Ok good. Any other blockers?
[06:07] Rajiv Menon: Nothing immediate. Let's make sure we get the sample set and the harness early.
[06:11] Maya Chen: Great. I'll recap next steps in a follow-up note. Thanks everyone.
[06:16] [meeting ends]
notes: Customer emphasized structured citation checks and low tolerance for critical hallucinations. Redwood proposed automated citation-extraction for hallucination detection and normalization rules for format variance. Agreement on daily regression during POC and a week-3 load sweep. IP allowlist and VPC peering to be validated in SE pairing session.
